Human beings are among a small group of mammals that have what are referred to a 'mirror neurons'; an ability to deduce the emotional state of other humans and animals by associating what we see happening to them to our own experience. In other words, if you see someone being hurt or acting playfully, you have this ability to imagine what they are feeling as if you were, yourself, feeling it. While you are observing this happening, the same areas of your own brain activate as if you were actually experiencing this yourself. This forms the basis of empathic awareness and emotional intelligence that is necessary for us to function as social animals. This is amplified by our ability to communicate and thus share feelings among each other.

Our culture builds morality deductively around our empathic sensibility and specific events that test it and encodes these deductions as mores, taboos, rules and laws. We recognize what is harmful to others by knowing what is harmful to us and what others communicate to us is harmful to them and project the potential outcome of actions in that context. If a situation is very common, we tend to invent some very specific rule about it. Some of these deductions are pretty obvious. Killing and physically harming others is pretty plain. Others are more subtle and complex, like stealing, sexual fidelity, and so on. Since it is both a talent and skill, not everyone has the same degree of emotional intelligence. Codifying morals in some ways helps to standardize behavior for those people who might be a bit poorer in empathic sensibility or have difficulty comprehending a situation in a mutual context. But there is a chronic hazard in this of abstraction and losing the memory of the context of the moral deduction. We sometimes end up with mores and taboos whose context is lost in time and we no longer know quite why they exist. To preserve these contexts, we have often created stories and legends and ultimately 'mythic systems' that can form the foundations of religions and a supernatural authority structure to rationalize these social rules. As society grows and cultures become more complex, so do their rules compelling their standardization as written laws and the creation of hierarchies of authority to administer and enforce them. This tends to grow in a cancerous fashion. It's far easier to invent laws than to obsolesce them and the system of logic which underlies them quickly becomes incoherent with constant reinterpretation of language.

We also have the problem of a number of people in our society who are lacking in empathic capacity or are able to willfully switch it on and off. We call these people sociopaths and consider this a personality disorder. This is sometimes suggested as the basis of criminal behavior. Some of these people we refer to as 'high functioning' sociopaths because they have high emotional intelligence despite their lack of empathy, allowing them to function 'well' in society despite their inability to actually relate to others in normal ways. This, however, leads to a compulsive tendency to manipulate, which makes these people potentially very destructive to a civil society in more subtle and far-reaching ways. Unfortunately, their manipulative skills tend to put them into positions of wealth and power. Politics and business in particular strongly select for sociopathy. We have very large concentrations of sociopathic personalities in the executive class, among lawyers, politicians, the military, police, religion, and other positions of authority--positions where people very rarely receive the kinds of psychological evaluations commonly imposed on lower classes of employment. High functioning sociopaths can be hard to detect but tend to reveal themselves in their impact on the environment around them and the wreckage they leave in their wake. Both Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton show quite plain signs of sociopathy, but this is not unexpected as it's really very unlikely that anyone can attain their status in our culture and society and not be a sociopath.

The foundations of morality have become very important in artificial intelligence and robotics as we now have recognized the need for our increasingly intelligent machines to also have emotional intelligence as well as a simply matter of safety. And so we are beginning to develop the machine equivalents to the mirror neurons, the empathic sensibility, we've developed as social animals. This is why some futurists have little concern for the supposed existential hazard of AI many fear as they anticipate future machine intelligence to well surpass us humans in empathy and emotional intelligence by desifn, hence the title of the futurist poem; All Watched-Over By Machines Of Loving Grace
